## **Biographies**  
**Charlotte Dennery**began her career as a Senior Official at INSEE, at the French Ministry of Economy and Finance, and then at the Budget Department. She joined BNPParibas as Head of Strategy and Development of Corporate and Investment Banking (2001-2002). She was then Head of Strategy and Development for the Group in the United States (2002-2004) and Chief Financial Officer and Head of Asset Management at BNPParibas Cardif (2004-2009). At BNPParibas Investment Partners from 2009 to 2015, she was Chief Executive Officer of FundQuest until 2013, and Chief Operating Officer from 2010 to 2015. In 2015, she was appointed Director and Chief Executive Officer of BNPParibas Leasing Solutions, the Group’s subsidiary specialized in the financing of professional equipment. Since 2021, Charlotte Dennery has been Director and Chief Executive Officer of BNPParibas Personal Finance and a member of the Executive Committee of BNPParibas. She has been a member of the French Association of Financial Companies (ASF) Board, which represents businesses in credit, financial services, and investment, since March 2024, where she held the role of Vice President. Charlotte Dennery is a graduate of Ecole Polytechnique and ENSAE ParisTech.
**Gilles Zeitoun**joined BNPParibas Personal Finance in 1994 where he spent most of his career, alternating between corporate roles and operational roles across countries.       "content": "# BNP Paribas Personal Finance : Charlotte Dennery passe la main à Gilles Zeitoun

BNP Paribas a annoncé, le 19 novembre 2025, une nouvelle organisation à la tête de sa filiale de crédit à la consommation, BNP Paribas Personal Finance. À compter du 1er janvier 2026, Charlotte Dennery deviendra présidente du conseil d’administration tout en occupant le rôle de senior advisor du pôle commercial, personal banking & services (CPBS).  
Elle sera remplacée à la direction exécutive par Gilles Zeitoun, nommé administrateur directeur général et futur membre du comité exécutif du groupe.  
Tous deux rapporteront à Thierry Laborde, directeur général délégué de BNP Paribas, en charge de CPBS. Il a également souligné la solidité retrouvée de BNP Paribas Personal Finance et la contribution de Charlotte Dennery au développement de nouveaux leviers transverses, notamment dans la mobilité et les paiements. Il a également exprimé sa confiance dans la capacité de Gilles Zeitoun à poursuivre et accélérer la transformation engagée, en cohérence avec le plan stratégique 2027-2030.
Diplômée de l’École polytechnique et de l’Ensae ParisTech, Charlotte Dennery a mené une carrière riche au sein du secteur public puis chez BNP Paribas. Passée par la Banque de financement et d’investissement (BFI), Cardif, Investment Partners et BNP Paribas Leasing Solutions, elle dirige BNP Paribas Personal Finance depuis 2021. Elle siège également au comité exécutif du groupe et est [membre du conseil de l’Association française des sociétés financières (ASF)](https://journalauto.com/services/charlotte-dennery-nouvelle-presidente-de-lasf/).  
Entré en 1994 chez BNP Paribas Personal Finance, Gilles Zeitoun connaît la maison. Il y a occupé des responsabilités variées, de la direction des risques en France à des postes de CEO à l’international, notamment en Roumanie, en Espagne et en Italie pour Findomestic.  
Depuis 2024, il occupait les fonctions de directeur général adjoint, puis de directeur général délégué en 2025, supervisant un périmètre étendu incluant la zone euro, le Royaume-Uni, les pays nordiques, ainsi que plusieurs géographies intégrées aux activités de banque de détail du groupe.

# BNP Paribas Leadership Organizational Structure and Responsibilities

BNP Paribas has a hierarchical leadership structure consisting of **General Management** and an **Executive Committee** with a total of **19 members** (as of 2024-2026). The Executive Committee meets at least once a week to set and implement the Group's strategy.

## General Management (6 Members)

### 1. **Jean-Laurent Bonnafé** - Director and Chief Executive Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Bears overall responsibility for the management of the Group with extensive powers. All operational activities and Group functions fall under his direct responsibility.
- Oversees the Group's overall strategy, including focus on eurozone operations
- Member of the Board of Directors since 2010
- Appointed CEO in December 2011

### 2. **Yann Gérardin** - Chief Operating Officer and Executive Chairman of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees Corporate & Institutional Banking division
- Leads CIB's strategic direction and operations
- Member of Executive Committee since 2011
- Appointed Chief Operating Officer in 2021

### 3. **Thierry Laborde** - Chief Operating Officer, in charge of Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS)
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees all retail banking activities including:
  - Domestic Markets (France, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg)
  - International Retail Banking
  - BNP Paribas Personal Finance
- Member of Executive Committee since 2011
- Appointed Chief Operating Officer in 2021

### 4. **Renaud Dumora** - Deputy Chief Operating Officer, in charge of Investment & Protection Services (IPS)
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees the IPS division, which includes:
  - Savings and investment activities
  - Protection services (insurance)
  - Real estate services
  - BNP Paribas Cardif (insurance)
  - BNP Paribas Asset Management
  - BNP Paribas Wealth Management
- Chairman of BNP Paribas Cardif
- Appointed Deputy Chief Operating Officer in 2021

### 5. **Yannick Jung** - Deputy Chief Operating Officer, in charge of Commercial & Personal Banking businesses in the euro zone within CPBS
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees Commercial & Personal Banking operations in the eurozone
- Manages retail banking activities across euro zone countries
- Previously Head of Corporate & Institutional Banking Global Banking (2023-2025)
- Appointed Deputy Chief Operating Officer in September 2025

### 6. **Olivier Osty** - Deputy Chief Operating Officer and Chief Executive Officer of Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB)
- **Responsibilities**: CEO of CIB division, managing:
  - Global Markets
  - Corporate banking operations
  - Investment banking activities
- Previously Head of CIB's Global Markets activity (2016-2025)
- Appointed Deputy Chief Operating Officer in September 2025

## Executive Committee Members - Business Line Heads (8 Members)

### 7. **Michael Anseeuw** - Director and Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Executive Board of BNP Paribas Fortis
- **Responsibilities**: Leads BNP Paribas Fortis (Belgium operations)
- Oversees retail banking in Belgium
- Appointed CEO of BNP Paribas Fortis in January 2023

### 8. **Isabelle Loc** - Head of BNP Paribas Commercial & Personal Banking in France
- **Responsibilities**: Manages all commercial and personal banking operations in France
- Oversees French retail banking network
- Previously Director and CEO of BNP Paribas Leasing Solutions (2021-2024)
- Appointed to current role in 2024

### 9. **Elena Goitini** - Chief Executive Officer of BNL
- **Responsibilities**: Leads BNL banca commerciale (Italy operations)
- Manages retail banking in Italy
- Previously Head of Private Banking and Wealth Management in Italy
- Appointed CEO of BNL in 2021

### 10. **Pauline Leclerc-Glorieux** - Director and Chief Executive Officer of BNP Paribas Cardif
- **Responsibilities**: Leads the Group's insurance business
- Oversees global insurance operations and strategy
- Previously Deputy CEO responsible for Efficiency, Technology and Operations at Cardif
- Appointed Director and CEO of BNP Paribas Cardif in 2021

### 11. **Gilles Zeitoun** - Director and Chief Executive Officer of BNP Paribas Personal Finance
- **Responsibilities**: Leads consumer credit operations across:
  - Eurozone countries
  - United Kingdom and Nordic countries
  - South Africa
  - Integrated business units in Poland, Turkey, Ukraine, Morocco, and Algeria
- Previously CEO of Findomestic (Italy) and Cetelem operations in Romania and Spain
- Appointed Director and CEO in January 2026

### 12. **Sandro Pierri** - Chief Executive Officer of BNP Paribas Asset Management
- **Responsibilities**: Leads the unified asset management platform (following merger with AXA Investment Managers)
- Oversees investment solutions for individual savers, companies, and institutions
- Manages over €1.6 trillion in assets under management
- Reports to Renaud Dumora
- Joined Executive Committee in March 2026

## Executive Committee Members - Central Functions (6 Members)

### 13. **Marc Camus** - Chief Information Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Leads Group IT strategy including:
  - IT system security
  - Operational efficiency
  - Artificial intelligence and cloud computing deployment
  - Digital transformation
- Previously CIO of BNP Paribas Fortis
- Reports to Philippe Maillard
- Appointed Group CIO in April 2025

### 14. **Lars Machenil** - Chief Financial Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees all financial functions including:
  - Group financial management
  - Financial reporting and control
  - Treasury operations
  - Investor relations
- Member of Executive Committee since 2012
- Appointed CFO in March 2012

### 15. **Frank Roncey** - Chief Risk Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Leads Group Risk Management including:
  - Credit risk management
  - Market and liquidity risk
  - Operational risk
  - Risk oversight across all business lines
- Member of Executive Committee since 2014
- Appointed Chief Risk Officer in 2014

### 16. **Stéphanie Maarek** - Chief Compliance Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees Group compliance including:
  - Regulatory compliance
  - Conduct and control
  - Non-financial risk management
- Previously Chief Conduct and Control Officer for Global Markets and CIB
- Appointed Chief Compliance Officer in January 2023

### 17. **Sarah Roussel** - Head of Human Resources
- **Responsibilities**: Leads HR strategy for 180,000 employees including:
  - Talent management and development
  - Organizational transformation
  - People strategy aligned with business priorities
- Previously CEO of Arval France
- Reports to Philippe Maillard
- Appointed Head of HR in July 2026

### 18. **Philippe Maillard** - Group Chief Operating Officer
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees Technology and Operational Performance including:
  - IT Group
  - Group Data Office
  - Facilities management
  - Procurement
  - Internal consulting
  - Operational efficiency and transformation
- Previously COO of Corporate & Institutional Banking
- Appointed Group COO in February 2025

### 19. **Elise Hermant** - Head of Communications
- **Responsibilities**: Leads Group communications and reputation management including:
  - Corporate communications
  - Brand management
  - Media relations
  - Strategic communication supporting the Group's strategic plan
- Reports directly to General Management
- Joined Executive Committee in July 2024

## Additional Executive Committee Members

### 20. **Anne Pointet** - Head of Company Engagement
- **Responsibilities**: Oversees Company Engagement including:
  - Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
  - Environmental and social inclusion initiatives
  - Sustainable development strategy
  - Corporate philanthropy coordination
- Supported by Laurence Pessez (Deputy Head, CSR) and Isabelle Giordano (Head of Group Philanthropy)
- Appointed Head of Company Engagement in July 2024

## Key Organizational Features

**Gender Diversity**: As of 2024, 42% of BNP Paribas' Executive Committee members are women, exceeding the Group's target of 40% by 2025.

**Meeting Frequency**: The Executive Committee meets at least once a week to coordinate operations, implement strategy, and manage risks.

**Reporting Structure**: All Executive Committee members ultimately report to Jean-Laurent Bonnafé, the CEO, who has extensive powers over all operational activities and Group functions.

**Strategic Focus**: The Executive Committee drives the Group's strategic plan focused on:
- Consolidating European leadership
- Sustainable finance and environmental transition
- Digital transformation and innovation
- Operational efficiency and profitability
- Client service excellence across all business lines

query: What is the average CET1 capital ratio and NPL ratio of EU banks in the latest quarter?
answer:
Based on the latest available data for EU banks:

## Q4 2025 (Latest Quarter)

**Average CET1 Capital Ratio: 16.3%**
- The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio for EU/EEA banks stood at 16.3% in Q4 2025 (transitional under CRR3), remaining stable throughout 2025
- Risk-weighted assets reached EUR 10.2 trillion in Q4 2025
- The CET1 ratio varied significantly across countries, ranging from 13.28% in Spain to 23.12% in Lithuania
- For ECB-supervised significant institutions specifically, the CET1 ratio was 16.18% in Q4 2025

**Average NPL Ratio: 1.8%**
- The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio stood at 1.8% in Q4 2025, representing the lowest level since the EBA began collecting this data
- Total NPL volumes declined slightly to EUR 370 billion
- This represents a significant improvement from 2.31% a year earlier (Q3 2024) and is down from a crisis-era peak of over 6% in 2015
- For ECB-supervised significant institutions, the NPL ratio was 2.18% in Q4 2025 (excluding cash balances at central banks)

## Additional Context

**Q1 2025 Data:**
- CET1 ratio: 16.2%
- NPL ratio: Approximately 1.84% (EBA data) to 2.22% (ECB supervisory data for significant institutions)
- NPL volumes: EUR 377.8 billion

**Q3 2025 Data:**
- CET1 ratio: 16.10%
- NPL ratio: 2.22% (ECB supervisory data for significant institutions)

The European banking sector demonstrates strong capital adequacy well above regulatory requirements (minimum 4.5% CET1, with 7.0% including capital conservation buffer) and significantly improved asset quality compared to historical levels.

query: What capital and liquidity (LCR) levels do significant institutions supervised by the ECB report?
answer:
Significant institutions supervised by the ECB report robust capital and liquidity levels that are well above regulatory requirements. Based on the most recent data available:

## Capital Levels

**Most Recent Data (Q4 2025):**
- Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio: 16.18%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.68%
- Total capital ratio: 20.32%

**Q3 2025:**
- CET1 ratio: 16.10%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.59%
- Total capital ratio: 20.24%

**Q4 2024:**
- CET1 ratio: 15.86%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.33%
- Total capital ratio: 19.99%

**Q3 2024:**
- CET1 ratio: 15.72%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.15%
- Total capital ratio: 19.81%

**Mid-2024:**
- Aggregate CET1 ratio: 15.8%

The CET1 ratio varies significantly across countries. In Q3 2024, it ranged from 12.82% in Spain to 22.76% in Latvia. In Q4 2024, the range was from 12.88% in Spain to 22.05% in Latvia. In Q4 2025, the CET1 ratio ranged across countries from 13.28% in Spain to 23.12% in Lithuania.

The aggregate CET1 ratio has shown significant improvement since the establishment of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in 2014. Starting from a level of 11.1% at year-end 2013, the aggregate CET1 ratio increased by 4.9 percentage points to 16.0% at year-end 2024.

## Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)

**Most Recent Data (Q4 2025):**
- LCR: 158.60%

**Q3 2025:**
- LCR: 156.73%

**Q2 2025:**
- LCR: 158% (as reported in SREP results)

**Q2 2026:**
- LCR: 154.91%

**Q4 2024:**
The LCR stood at 217% for less significant institutions (LSIs) and 164% for significant institutions (SIs) in Q4 2023, well above the regulatory minimum target of 100%.

The LCR has remained consistently above 150% for significant institutions in the euro area since the coronavirus (COVID-19) period. The regulatory minimum requirement is 100%, and banks are expected to maintain this as a minimum in normal times. During periods of stress, banks would be expected to use their pool of liquid assets, thereby temporarily falling below the minimum requirement.

The LCR decreased from 157.88% in Q2 2025 to 156.73% in Q3 2025, primarily driven by a €37 billion (1.15%) increase in net liquidity outflow. The LCR also showed a decline from 158.50% one year prior to Q3 2025.

## Overall Capital Requirements

As of 2026, the aggregate required CET1 ratio of significant institutions stands at around 11.2%, which is close to the pre-pandemic level observed in 2019. The overall CET1 capital requirement and guidance and Pillar 2 requirements applicable in 2026 remained broadly stable at 11.2% and 1.2% respectively.

Capital headroom compared with overall capital requirements has remained broadly stable. In 2025, 85% of institutions were expected to have capital headroom of over 200 basis points; only a few were projected to have capital headroom below 100 basis points.

These figures demonstrate that significant institutions supervised by the ECB maintain robust capital and liquidity buffers that significantly exceed regulatory minimums, providing substantial resilience against financial stress.

      "content": "**The BCBS established the LCR standard in 2013.** The LCR aims to ensure that banks maintain a liquidity buffer on their balance sheets which can be liquidated quickly during a period of liquidity stress.\\[[1](#footnote.1)] In particular, the LCR is a forward-looking measure which requires banks to hold a sufficient stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) that can be converted into cash easily and immediately to survive a period of significant liquidity stress lasting 30 calendar days:  \nThe EU implemented the LCR in line with the Basel Framework requirements and applies it to all banking institutions in the EU, by default at both consolidated and individual level.       "content": "In the wake of the global financial crisis of 2008, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision introduced a comprehensive set of reform measures known as Basel III. These reforms aim to strengthen the regulation, supervision, and risk management of banks.  \nOne of the cornerstone components of Basel III is the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), a critical metric designed to ensure that Banks and Financial Institutions maintain adequate liquidity buffers to withstand periods of financial stress.  \n**Understanding Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)**  \nThe Liquidity Coverage Ratio is a key liquidity standard established to promote short-term resilience by ensuring that banks have sufficient high-quality liquid assets (HQLAs) to cover their total net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. In simple terms, LCR is a stress test that assesses a bank's ability to survive a month-long period of significant liquidity stress.  \n**Few Components of LCR**  \nHigh-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLAs):  \nHQLAs are assets that can be easily and quickly converted into cash with little or no loss of value.  \nTotal Net Cash Outflows:  \nThis component represents the total expected cash outflows minus the total expected cash inflows during the 30-day stress period. Outflows include deposits, debt securities, and other liabilities, while inflows comprise contractual inflows from outstanding exposures.\nTo comply with Basel III, Banks and Financial Institutions must maintain an LCR of at least 100%, meaning they should have enough HQLAs to cover their net cash outflows for 30 days.  \n**Importance of LCR Enhanced Liquidity Management:** The LCR encourages banks to improve their liquidity risk management practices, ensuring they are better prepared for periods of financial stress. By holding a sufficient buffer of HQLAs, banks can avoid liquidity crunches that could lead to severe economic disruptions.  \nMarket Confidence:  \nA robust LCR enhances the confidence of depositors, investors, and other market participants in the stability of the banking system. Knowing that banks have adequate liquidity to manage short-term stress periods helps maintain trust and stability in the financial markets.  \nRegulatory Compliance:  \nAdherence to LCR requirements is mandatory for banks operating under Basel III regulations. Non-compliance can result in regulatory sanctions, including restrictions on dividends, share buybacks, and other capital distributions.  \n**Challenges in Implementing LCR**  \nWhile the LCR is crucial for ensuring liquidity resilience, its implementation poses several challenges for banks:  \nCost of Compliance:  \nMaintaining a high stock of HQLAs can be costly for banks, as these assets typically yield lower returns compared to other investments. Balancing profitability with regulatory compliance is a significant challenge.  \nOperational Complexity:\nOperational Complexity:  \nThe calculation and monitoring of LCR require sophisticated risk management systems and processes. Banks need to invest in technology and human resources to ensure accurate and timely reporting.  \nMarket Conditions:  \nDuring periods of market stress, the value and liquidity of HQLAs can fluctuate. Banks must continuously assess and adjust their portfolios to maintain the required LCR levels.  \n**Conclusion**  \nThe Liquidity Coverage Ratio is a vital component of the Basel III framework, aimed at ensuring that banks maintain adequate liquidity buffers to navigate short-term financial stress. While the LCR enhances the stability and resilience of the banking sector, its implementation requires careful planning and management.  \nBy understanding the essentials of LCR and addressing the associated challenges, banks can better position themselves to weather financial storms and contribute to a more stable and secure global financial system.  \n**Surya's BASEL III Liquidity Ratio Solution is compliant with the BCBS regulations in monitoring and enhancing the Liquidity Risk Management for Banks and Financial Institutions.**  \nSubscribe for updates and stay informed with our latest insights, news, stories, and announcements.",

      "content": "# Basel III: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio and liquidity risk monitoring tools  \n### This version  \n[PDF full text (431kb)](https://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs238.pdf) | 75 pages  \n[Liquidity risk](https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publications.htm?bcbspubls_topics=Liquidity%20risk)\n### Note  \nThis standard has been integrated into the consolidated  \n[Basel Framework](https://www.bis.org/basel_framework/).  \nThe Basel Committee issued the full text of the revised Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) following [endorsement on 6 January 2013](https://www.bis.org/press/p130106.htm) by its governing body - the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS).       "content": "# Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) Explained  \n[Hazem Alhalabi](https://b2broker.com/author/hazem-alhalabi/)  \n[Tamta Suladze](https://b2broker.com/author/tamta-suladze/)  \nSudden changes in user demands, especially during economic meltdowns or public panic, can massively impact financial institutions. It safeguards the rights of institutions and consumers.  \nLet’s explain the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) rule and why it has become a necessary tool.\n## What is The Liquidity Coverage Ratio?  \nThe Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is a regulatory standard introduced by the [Basel III international framework](https://www.bis.org/bcbs/basel3.htm) to ensure banks maintain adequate high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to meet short-term obligations.  \nIt is designed to enable banks and financial institutions to withstand a 30-day stress scenario by having a liquidity coverage of at least 100%.  \nThis system mitigates [liquidity risks](https://b2broker.com/news/liquidity-gap/) and enhances economic stability, offering a safeguard against potential financial crises and failures.       "content": "## IMF Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) April 2026: Bank Liquidity Analysis  \nThe **April 2026 Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR)** underscores a global financial system navigating a \"perfect storm.\" While structural reforms have left the banking sector well-capitalized, the escalation of conflict in the Middle East has triggered a sharp spike in energy prices and renewed inflationary pressures.  \nCentral to the IMF’s assessment is the **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)**. This strength is underpinned by several structural advantages:  \n- **Positive Yield Shift:**The Bank of Japan’s (BoJ) decision to maintain benchmark rates at**0.75%**has attracted significant capital back into yen-denominated assets. This has replenished bank liquidity as domestic investors repatriate funds from overseas markets.\n- **Massive Cash Reserves:**Japanese banks continue to hold vast amounts of excess reserves at the central bank.       "content": "You will be redirected to the website of our parent company, Schönherr Rechtsanwälte GmbH: [www.schoenherr.eu](https://www.schoenherr.eu)  \n- 01 February 2021\n- roadmap\n- austria  \n**Already at an early stage of the COVID‑19 crisis the European Central Bank (ECB) adopted several supervisory relief measures to allow banks to absorb losses and keep lending to the real economy.**  \nOn 12 March 2020, the ECB announced that it will allow banks to temporarily use capital and liquidity buffers which they have built in past years to enjoy more flexibility during the COVID‑19 crisis.       "content": "## The balance between fixed rules and flexible measures  
Rules derived from the prescriptive elements of the Basel standards account for around two-thirds of EU capital requirements. They include the definition and measurement of risk‑weighted assets, the minimum capital ratios under Pillar 1, the capital conservation buffer and the global systemically important institution (G‑SII) buffer. These elements are largely fixed in legislation and apply in a harmonised way across the EU.  
Around one-third of capital requirements come from non‑prescriptive (“principles-based”) Basel elements that are implemented and calibrated at EU or national level. This includes microprudential measures set by the ECB, such as the Pillar 2 requirement which captures risks not fully covered under Pillar 1, and the Pillar 2 guidance which is designed to cover potential stress scenarios and emerging risks that may not yet be fully quantifiable or apparent. It also includes macroprudential measures, such as the countercyclical capital buffer and buffers for other systemically important institutions (O-SIIs). Macroprudential measures remain largely decentralised: they are set by national macroprudential authorities, with a limited role for the ECB in “topping-up” requirements where necessary.

These increases, however, have not significantly impeded banks from granting new loans. Recent ECB research shows that macroprudential capital buffer increases since the pandemic have only had a modest impact on aggregate credit supply, as banks have benefited from sufficient capital headroom to be able to absorb the higher requirements without cutting back on lending.\[[3](#footnote.3)]  
As at 2026, the aggregate required Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of significant institutions stands at around 11.2%, which is close to the pre‑pandemic level observed in 2019. Recent regulatory changes, including the implementation of the final Basel III reforms, have had only a limited impact on requirements in the short term. Transitional arrangements will smooth the effects until full phase‑in, which is expected to be completed by 2032. Banks have generally been able to meet the higher requirements without difficulty, reflecting strong capital positions built up over time.
In summary, maintaining robust capital requirements remains critical for ensuring that banks can lend reliably across cycles, without compromising profitability or investor confidence. The evidence supports a prudent approach that resists calls for reduced capital standards, recognising that strong capital positions benefit both banks and the wider economy in the long run.

Significant institutions supervised by the ECB report robust capital and liquidity levels that are well above regulatory requirements. Based on the most recent data available:

## Capital Levels

**Most Recent Data (Q4 2025):**
- Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio: 16.18%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.68%
- Total capital ratio: 20.32%

**Q3 2025:**
- CET1 ratio: 16.10%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.59%
- Total capital ratio: 20.24%

**Q4 2024:**
- CET1 ratio: 15.86%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.33%
- Total capital ratio: 19.99%

**Q3 2024:**
- CET1 ratio: 15.72%
- Tier 1 ratio: 17.15%
- Total capital ratio: 19.81%

**Mid-2024:**
- Aggregate CET1 ratio: 15.8%

The CET1 ratio varies significantly across countries. In Q3 2024, it ranged from 12.82% in Spain to 22.76% in Latvia. In Q4 2024, the range was from 12.88% in Spain to 22.05% in Latvia. In Q4 2025, the CET1 ratio ranged across countries from 13.28% in Spain to 23.12% in Lithuania.

The aggregate CET1 ratio has shown significant improvement since the establishment of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in 2014. Starting from a level of 11.1% at year-end 2013, the aggregate CET1 ratio increased by 4.9 percentage points to 16.0% at year-end 2024.

## Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)

**Most Recent Data (Q4 2025):**
- LCR: 158.60%

**Q3 2025:**
- LCR: 156.73%

**Q2 2025:**
- LCR: 158% (as reported in SREP results)

**Q2 2026:**
- LCR: 154.91%

**Q4 2024:**
The LCR stood at 217% for less significant institutions (LSIs) and 164% for significant institutions (SIs) in Q4 2023, well above the regulatory minimum target of 100%.

The LCR has remained consistently above 150% for significant institutions in the euro area since the coronavirus (COVID-19) period. The regulatory minimum requirement is 100%, and banks are expected to maintain this as a minimum in normal times. During periods of stress, banks would be expected to use their pool of liquid assets, thereby temporarily falling below the minimum requirement.

The LCR decreased from 157.88% in Q2 2025 to 156.73% in Q3 2025, primarily driven by a €37 billion (1.15%) increase in net liquidity outflow. The LCR also showed a decline from 158.50% one year prior to Q3 2025.

## Overall Capital Requirements

As of 2026, the aggregate required CET1 ratio of significant institutions stands at around 11.2%, which is close to the pre-pandemic level observed in 2019. The overall CET1 capital requirement and guidance and Pillar 2 requirements applicable in 2026 remained broadly stable at 11.2% and 1.2% respectively.

Capital headroom compared with overall capital requirements has remained broadly stable. In 2025, 85% of institutions were expected to have capital headroom of over 200 basis points; only a few were projected to have capital headroom below 100 basis points.

These figures demonstrate that significant institutions supervised by the ECB maintain robust capital and liquidity buffers that significantly exceed regulatory minimums, providing substantial resilience against financial stress.

query: What has been the trend of Spain's GDP, inflation (HICP) and unemployment in recent years?
answer:
Spain has experienced strong economic performance in recent years across GDP growth, inflation (HICP), and unemployment, though with varying trends for each indicator.

## GDP Growth Trends

Spain's GDP has shown robust growth, particularly outperforming other major European economies:

**2020-2024 Performance:**
- 2020: GDP fell by 10.94% (some sources cite -10.2% to -11.2%), marking the largest annual contraction in 45 years due to the COVID-19 pandemic
- 2021: Strong recovery with GDP growth of 6.4% to 6.68%
- 2022: Growth of 5.8% (revised upward from initial 5.5%)
- 2023: GDP grew by 2.5% to 2.7%
- 2024: Exceptional growth of 3.2% to 3.5% (various sources cite figures in this range), making Spain one of the fastest-growing advanced economies

**Recent Quarterly Performance:**
- Q3 2024: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.5% year-on-year
- Q4 2024: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.5% year-on-year
- Q1 2025: 0.6% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.2% year-on-year
- Q2 2025: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.1% year-on-year

**Key Drivers:**
- Strong domestic demand, contributing 3.6 percentage points to annual GDP growth in 2024
- Robust tourism sector, with an estimated 94 million international tourists in 2024 (10% increase from 2023)
- Household consumption growth of 3.5% year-on-year in 2024
- EU recovery funds deployment
- Strong labor market supporting household incomes
- Services sector providing over two-thirds of economic output

**Comparative Performance:**
Spain significantly outperformed other major European economies in 2024:
- Spain: 3.2%
- Germany: -0.2% (contraction)
- France: 1.1%
- Italy: 0.7%

**GDP Levels:**
- 2024 GDP: €1,594,330 million ($1,725,672 million)
- GDP per capita (2024): $35,239 to $36,190 (depending on source)
- Spain's GDP stood 7.6% above pre-pandemic levels by end of 2024

**Future Projections:**
- 2025: Growth forecast at 2.3% to 2.7% (various estimates)
- 2026: Projected growth of 1.8% to 2.2%
- OECD projects 2.6% growth for Spain in 2025, compared to 0.4% for Germany, 0.8% for France, and 0.7% for Italy

## Inflation (HICP) Trends

Spain's inflation has shown a complex pattern with periods of acceleration and moderation:

**Recent Annual Rates:**
- 2023: Average inflation of 3.5%
- 2024: Average inflation of 2.75% to 2.9%
- June 2024: 3.2% year-on-year
- July 2024: 3.5% to 3.6% year-on-year (revised upward)
- August 2024: 4.5% to 4.6% year-on-year
- December 2024: 3% year-on-year (with acceleration in shorter-term measures)

**Monthly Trends (2024-2026):**
- December 2024: 0.4% month-on-month (after 0.5% in both October and November)
- January 2025: 0.9% month-on-month spike
- February 2025: 0.4% month-on-month
- March 2026: 3.4% year-on-year (upwardly revised by 0.1pp)
- June 2026: 0.6% month-on-month rise, 3.6% year-on-year
- July 2026: -0.1% month-on-month, 3.5% to 3.6% year-on-year
- August 2026: 0.6% month-on-month, 4.5% year-on-year

**Acceleration Pattern:**
Spain's inflation has shown clear acceleration in shorter-term measures:
- 12-month rate: 3%
- 6-month annualized rate: 4% to 4.5%
- 3-month annualized rate: 5.7% to 5.8%

**Key Drivers:**
- Energy prices, particularly fuel costs (diesel inflation reached 15.7% year-on-year in July 2026, petrol 7.3%)
- Services inflation remaining sticky and elevated
- Transport inflation accelerating to 6.0% year-on-year
- Food price pressures
- Hospitality sector inflation at 4.8%
- Recreation and culture at 3.7%

**Core Inflation:**
Core inflation (excluding energy) has been more moderate but still above the ECB's 2% target:
- Generally ranging between 2.4% to 2.6% year-on-year
- Domestic CPI excluding energy: 2.6% over 12 months, 3.1% over 6 months

**Context:**
- Spain's inflation remains above the European Central Bank's 2% target
- Spain's inflation rate is above the eurozone average of approximately 2.5%
- The ECB uses HICP as its primary measure for monetary policy decisions
- Over 50% of price categories showed acceleration over three-month periods in recent data

## Unemployment Trends

Spain has achieved remarkable progress in reducing unemployment, though it remains elevated compared to European peers:

**Recent Unemployment Rates:**
- 2020: 16.13% (pandemic peak)
- 2021: 15.98% (Q1), declining to 13.33% (Q4)
- 2022: 12.87% (Q4)
- 2023: 12.18% average, 11.76% (Q4)
- 2024: 11.40% average, 10.61% (Q4)
- 2025: 10.38% average, 9.93% (Q4) - first time below 10% in 17 years
- Q1 2026: 10.83% (rose above 10% again)
- Q2 2026: 9.87% - lowest level since 2008 (18-year low)

**Employment Growth:**
- 2021: 840,700 new jobs created
- 2024: Over 500,000 new registered workers added
- Q2 2026: 486,000 jobs created, bringing total employment to 22.779 million (record high)
- Total employment reached 22.293 million in Q1 2026

**Labor Force Trends:**
- Labor force exceeded 25 million people for the first time in 2026
- Q2 2026: Labor force grew by 272,700 people
- Labor force participation rate rising, reaching 74.6% in Q1 2024

**Sectoral Performance:**
- Services sector (especially tourism) has been the primary driver of job creation
- Construction and industry also contributed to employment growth
- Agriculture sector has seen worker declines
- Healthcare and social services added 72,100 jobs year-on-year
- Education added 45,500 workers
- Financial and insurance sector added 47,800 new jobs

**Job Quality Improvements:**
- Almost three-quarters of employees now have permanent contracts
- Shift from temporary to permanent employment arrangements
- Full-time employment has increased significantly

**Challenges:**
- Q1 2026 saw the worst first quarter since COVID-19, with 231,500 more unemployed and 170,300 jobs lost
- Spain still has the highest unemployment rate in the European Union
- Youth unemployment remains particularly high (though specific recent rates vary by age group)
- Unemployment rate of 16-19 year-olds historically very elevated
- Regional disparities exist, with Basque Country having much lower unemployment than Andalusia and Canary Islands

**Historical Context:**
- Unemployment peaked at 27% in 2013 during the financial crisis
- Spain's unemployment rate has historically been about double the developed country average
- The country has made significant progress from the 2013 peak of approximately 6.28 million unemployed

**Future Projections:**
- Government forecast: unemployment to fall to 10.3% by end of 2026, and 8.7% by 2028
- Bank of Spain and various forecasts project continued gradual decline

**Comparative Position:**
- Spain's 10.38% (2025) compares unfavorably to EU peers like Malta (2.90%), Czechia (2.83%), and Germany (3.71%)
- Spain remains the second-highest unemployment rate in the EU after Greece

## Summary

Spain has demonstrated strong economic resilience in recent years with GDP growth significantly outpacing European peers, driven by tourism, domestic consumption, and EU recovery funds. However, inflation has proven stickier than desired, remaining above the ECB's 2% target with recent acceleration in shorter-term measures. Unemployment has improved dramatically from crisis peaks, reaching 18-year lows, though it remains the highest in the EU and faces challenges including high youth unemployment and regional disparities. The overall trend shows an economy in recovery with improving fundamentals, but with persistent structural challenges particularly in the labor market and ongoing inflationary pressures.

Unlike national CPI measures (which differ in basket composition, owner-occupied housing treatment, and geographic coverage), HICP applies a consistent methodology across all 27 member states, making genuine cross-country comparison possible. Energy carries roughly 15% of the HICP basket weight in the Baltic states, compared to around 10% in Western EU economies, explaining why energy price shocks registered so much more sharply in Tallinn and Riga than in Paris or Amsterdam. The ECB's 2% inflation target is defined in HICP terms at the euro area aggregate level — meaning that even when several eurozone members run well above or below target, the ECB responds to the area-wide average.
## Historical Context: From Deflation Fear to Inflation Shock  
The 2022–23 European inflation surge arrived against a backdrop that could hardly have been more different. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, the EU spent the better part of a decade battling not inflation but its opposite: deflation risk. With demand chronically weak, oil prices collapsing in 2014–16, and the eurozone experiencing near-zero or negative price growth, the ECB introduced negative interest rates and quantitative easing precisely to push inflation back up toward its 2% target. Between 2014 and 2020, EU HICP averaged well below 1.5% — and the academic consensus, reflected in ECB forward guidance, was that structural forces (globalisation, ageing populations, technology) would keep inflation low indefinitely.
## Frequently Asked Questions  
### What is HICP and how does the EU measure inflation?  
HICP stands for Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices — the EU's standardised inflation measure, calculated using the same methodology across all 27 member states to ensure comparability. It tracks a basket of goods and services purchased by households, with weights reflecting actual consumption patterns. Unlike national CPI measures (which differ in methodology), HICP allows direct cross-country comparison and is the benchmark the European Central Bank uses to define its 2% inflation target. Annual HICP inflation above 2% generally triggers ECB tightening; persistent below-target inflation may prompt stimulus. The ECB targets inflation at the euro area level, meaning individual eurozone members cannot adjust rates to address their domestic inflation rates.",

Spain's Unemployment Rate reflects a percentage of unemployed residents in relation to the total civilian labor force. The index covers unemployed citizens of appropriate age, having conditions and possibilities for employment, i.e. the working-age population. The Unemployment Rate is a very important indicator showing the number of people without any work. Related data is collected form a survey of working-age population. Households are surveyed quarterly and are asked about their current jobs. The Unemployment Rate index is calculated as the number of unemployed (aged 16 and over, not working and looking for a job) divided by the number of active population (economically active population aged 16 and over, employed and not employed) and is expressed as a percentage. In other words, the Unemployment Rate is not expressed in the ratio between the total number of unemployed people and the entire population, but only with respect to the country's total civilian labor force.  
This survey classifies a population of 16 years and older into 4 groups:  
- Employed: people having a paid work, as well as those on annual or sick leaves or strikes.
- Employed: people having a paid work, as well as those on annual or sick leaves or strikes.
- Unemployed: people who are not engaged in any labor activity, but who are actively seeking employment or waiting to get back to work. A person is considered unemployed if: 1) he or she is not working and has been actively looking for a job during the last four weeks; 2) he or she has been removed from work and is awaiting recovery, or 3) he or she is waiting to start working next month. In addition, the person must confirm that he or she is really looking for a job (such as visited local businesses, responded to job ads, etc.).
- Inactive population: category of adult population, which includes people involved in housekeeping, as well as pupils and students, retirees, people not able to work and those not looking for work.
- Active population: employed and unemployed citizens.  
The population census is considered not to be a suitable source for measuring this index, as opposed to household surveys. This survey provides a more advanced method, since it takes into account part-time employment, informal or seasonal work and occasional part-time work.

## GDP Growth Trends

Spain's GDP has shown robust growth, particularly outperforming other major European economies:

- 2024: Exceptional growth of 3.2% to 3.5% (various sources cite figures in this range), making Spain one of the fastest-growing advanced economies

- Q3 2024: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.5% year-on-year
- Q4 2024: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.5% year-on-year
- Q1 2025: 0.6% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.2% year-on-year
- Q2 2025: 0.8% quarter-on-quarter growth, 3.1% year-on-year

**Key Drivers:**
- Strong domestic demand, contributing 3.6 percentage points to annual GDP growth in 2024
- Robust tourism sector, with an estimated 94 million international tourists in 2024 (10% increase from 2023)
- Household consumption growth of 3.5% year-on-year in 2024
- EU recovery funds deployment
- Strong labor market supporting household incomes
- Services sector providing over two-thirds of economic output

**Comparative Performance:**
Spain significantly outperformed other major European economies in 2024:
- Spain: 3.2%
- Germany: -0.2% (contraction)
- France: 1.1%
- Italy: 0.7%

**GDP Levels:**
- 2024 GDP: €1,594,330 million ($1,725,672 million)
- GDP per capita (2024): $35,239 to $36,190 (depending on source)
- Spain's GDP stood 7.6% above pre-pandemic levels by end of 2024

**Future Projections:**
- 2025: Growth forecast at 2.3% to 2.7% (various estimates)
- 2026: Projected growth of 1.8% to 2.2%
- OECD projects 2.6% growth for Spain in 2025, compared to 0.4% for Germany, 0.8% for France, and 0.7% for Italy

## Inflation (HICP) Trends

Spain's inflation has shown a complex pattern with periods of acceleration and moderation:

**Recent Annual Rates:**
- 2023: Average inflation of 3.5%
- 2024: Average inflation of 2.75% to 2.9%
- June 2024: 3.2% year-on-year
- July 2024: 3.5% to 3.6% year-on-year (revised upward)
- August 2024: 4.5% to 4.6% year-on-year
- December 2024: 3% year-on-year (with acceleration in shorter-term measures)

**Monthly Trends (2024-2026):**
- December 2024: 0.4% month-on-month (after 0.5% in both October and November)
- January 2025: 0.9% month-on-month spike
- February 2025: 0.4% month-on-month
- March 2026: 3.4% year-on-year (upwardly revised by 0.1pp)
- June 2026: 0.6% month-on-month rise, 3.6% year-on-year
- July 2026: -0.1% month-on-month, 3.5% to 3.6% year-on-year
- August 2026: 0.6% month-on-month, 4.5% year-on-year

**Acceleration Pattern:**
Spain's inflation has shown clear acceleration in shorter-term measures:
- 12-month rate: 3%
- 6-month annualized rate: 4% to 4.5%
- 3-month annualized rate: 5.7% to 5.8%

**Key Drivers:**
- Energy prices, particularly fuel costs (diesel inflation reached 15.7% year-on-year in July 2026, petrol 7.3%)
- Services inflation remaining sticky and elevated
- Transport inflation accelerating to 6.0% year-on-year
- Food price pressures
- Hospitality sector inflation at 4.8%
- Recreation and culture at 3.7%

**Core Inflation:**
Core inflation (excluding energy) has been more moderate but still above the ECB's 2% target:
- Generally ranging between 2.4% to 2.6% year-on-year
- Domestic CPI excluding energy: 2.6% over 12 months, 3.1% over 6 months

**Context:**
- Spain's inflation remains above the European Central Bank's 2% target
- Spain's inflation rate is above the eurozone average of approximately 2.5%
- The ECB uses HICP as its primary measure for monetary policy decisions
- Over 50% of price categories showed acceleration over three-month periods in recent data

## Unemployment Trends

Spain has achieved remarkable progress in reducing unemployment, though it remains elevated compared to European peers:

**Recent Unemployment Rates:**
- 2020: 16.13% (pandemic peak)
- 2021: 15.98% (Q1), declining to 13.33% (Q4)
- 2022: 12.87% (Q4)
- 2023: 12.18% average, 11.76% (Q4)
- 2024: 11.40% average, 10.61% (Q4)
- 2025: 10.38% average, 9.93% (Q4) - first time below 10% in 17 years
- Q1 2026: 10.83% (rose above 10% again)
- Q2 2026: 9.87% - lowest level since 2008 (18-year low)

**Employment Growth:**
- 2021: 840,700 new jobs created
- 2024: Over 500,000 new registered workers added
- Q2 2026: 486,000 jobs created, bringing total employment to 22.779 million (record high)
- Total employment reached 22.293 million in Q1 2026

**Labor Force Trends:**
- Labor force exceeded 25 million people for the first time in 2026
- Q2 2026: Labor force grew by 272,700 people
- Labor force participation rate rising, reaching 74.6% in Q1 2024

**Sectoral Performance:**
- Services sector (especially tourism) has been the primary driver of job creation
- Construction and industry also contributed to employment growth
- Agriculture sector has seen worker declines
- Healthcare and social services added 72,100 jobs year-on-year
- Education added 45,500 workers
- Financial and insurance sector added 47,800 new jobs

**Job Quality Improvements:**
- Almost three-quarters of employees now have permanent contracts
- Shift from temporary to permanent employment arrangements
- Full-time employment has increased significantly

**Challenges:**
- Q1 2026 saw the worst first quarter since COVID-19, with 231,500 more unemployed and 170,300 jobs lost
- Spain still has the highest unemployment rate in the European Union
- Youth unemployment remains particularly high (though specific recent rates vary by age group)
- Unemployment rate of 16-19 year-olds historically very elevated
- Regional disparities exist, with Basque Country having much lower unemployment than Andalusia and Canary Islands

**Historical Context:**
- Unemployment peaked at 27% in 2013 during the financial crisis
- Spain's unemployment rate has historically been about double the developed country average
- The country has made significant progress from the 2013 peak of approximately 6.28 million unemployed

**Future Projections:**
- Government forecast: unemployment to fall to 10.3% by end of 2026, and 8.7% by 2028
- Bank of Spain and various forecasts project continued gradual decline

**Comparative Position:**
- Spain's 10.38% (2025) compares unfavorably to EU peers like Malta (2.90%), Czechia (2.83%), and Germany (3.71%)
- Spain remains the second-highest unemployment rate in the EU after Greece

## Summary

Spain has demonstrated strong economic resilience in recent years with GDP growth significantly outpacing European peers, driven by tourism, domestic consumption, and EU recovery funds. However, inflation has proven stickier than desired, remaining above the ECB's 2% target with recent acceleration in shorter-term measures. Unemployment has improved dramatically from crisis peaks, reaching 18-year lows, though it remains the highest in the EU and faces challenges including high youth unemployment and regional disparities. The overall trend shows an economy in recovery with improving fundamentals, but with persistent structural challenges particularly in the labor market and ongoing inflationary pressures.

query: What is the ECB's official interest rate and the latest M3 monetary aggregate?
answer:
Based on the latest available data from the European Central Bank (ECB):

## ECB Official Interest Rates

The ECB's current official interest rates are:

- **Deposit Facility Rate: 2.00%** (effective since June 11, 2025)
- **Main Refinancing Operations Rate: 2.15%**
- **Marginal Lending Facility Rate: 2.40%**

The deposit facility rate is the primary tool the ECB uses to steer monetary policy stance. The ECB has kept these rates unchanged since June 2025, marking multiple consecutive holds after completing an easing cycle that began in June 2024. During that cycle, the ECB cut rates eight times, reducing the deposit facility rate from 4.00% (September 2023 peak) to the current 2.00%.

## Latest M3 Monetary Aggregate

The most recent M3 monetary aggregate data shows:

- **July 2026: 3.4%** annual growth rate (latest available)
- **June 2026: 3.3%** annual growth rate
- **May 2026: 3.2%** annual growth rate
- **March 2026: 3.2%** annual growth rate
- **January 2026: 3.3%** annual growth rate
- **December 2025: 2.8%** annual growth rate

The M3 monetary aggregate, which includes currency in circulation, overnight deposits, short-term deposits up to 2 years, money market fund shares, and short-term debt securities, stood at 3.4% year-on-year growth in July 2026. This represents a slight increase from 3.3% in June 2026.

The narrower M1 aggregate (currency in circulation and overnight deposits) decreased to 3.1% in July 2026 from 3.5% in June 2026. Short-term deposits other than overnight deposits (M2-M1) increased to 3.8% in July from 2.8% in June, while marketable instruments (M3-M2) decreased to 4.2% from 4.4%.

The money supply is one of the most important variables of an economy. Although there is no uniform definition, it is always classified according to availability and the next higher category includes all lower ones. The ECB defines the first category of monetary aggregates, M0, as circulating currency, i.e. coins and notes, M1 as M0 plus funds on current accounts (payable on demand), M2 as M1 plus fixed-term deposits up to 2 years and savings deposits redeemable at notice at a maximum of 3 months and finally M3 as M2 plus shares in money market funds or securities and repurchase agreements and debt securities with a maturity of up to 2 years. Of these different monetary aggregates, M3 is the most important as it is the most stable. If, for example, only the savings interest rate changes, M1 and M2 are redeployed, but M3 remains constant.
In general, a positive relationship is assumed between the growth of money supply M3 and that of inflation, economic growth and income. This means that an insufficient money supply M3 has negative influences on the other three economic variables. An increase in M3 should therefore have a positive impact on the currency, as income and inflation will also increase as a result.

query: How have the federal funds rate and the US unemployment rate evolved over the last 24 months?
answer:
Over the last 24 months (approximately March 2023 to March 2025), both the federal funds rate and the US unemployment rate have shown significant evolution, reflecting the Federal Reserve's monetary policy response to inflation and the resulting labor market dynamics.

## Federal Funds Rate Evolution (March 2023 - March 2025)

**The Tightening Phase (March 2023 - July 2023):**
The Federal Reserve continued its aggressive rate hiking campaign in early 2023. In March 2023, the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to a target range of 4.75% - 5.00%. This was followed by another 25 basis point increase in May 2023, bringing the rate to 5.00% - 5.25%. The final rate hike of the cycle occurred in July 2023, with a 25 basis point increase to 5.25% - 5.50%, marking a 22-year high.

**The Extended Pause (July 2023 - September 2024):**
After reaching the peak rate of 5.25% - 5.50% in July 2023, the Federal Reserve held rates steady for over a year. The FOMC paused rates at eight consecutive meetings between July 2023 and July 2024, maintaining the 5.25% - 5.50% target range. During this period, the effective federal funds rate remained at approximately 5.33%.

**The Cutting Cycle Begins (September 2024 - March 2025):**
In September 2024, the Fed initiated its first rate cut in nearly three years with a significant 50 basis point reduction, bringing the rate to 4.75% - 5.00%. This was followed by two additional 25 basis point cuts: one in November 2024 (to 4.50% - 4.75%) and another in December 2024 (to 4.25% - 4.50%). The Fed then held rates steady at 4.25% - 4.50% through January and March 2025 meetings.

By March 2025, the federal funds rate stood at 4.25% - 4.50%, representing a cumulative reduction of 100 basis points from the peak, though still significantly elevated compared to pre-2022 levels.

## US Unemployment Rate Evolution (March 2023 - March 2025)

**Low and Stable Period (March 2023 - July 2023):**
The unemployment rate remained remarkably low during the first half of 2023. In March 2023, it stood at 3.5%, and reached a 50-year low of 3.4% in April 2023. The rate remained between 3.4% and 3.7% through July 2023, with June 2023 at 3.6% and July 2023 at 3.5%.

**Gradual Increase Phase (August 2023 - December 2023):**
Beginning in August 2023, the unemployment rate began a gradual upward trend. It increased to 3.8% in August, September, and October 2023, before settling at 3.7% for November and December 2023.

**Continued Rise (January 2024 - December 2024):**
Throughout 2024, the unemployment rate continued its upward trajectory. It remained at 3.7% in January 2024, then increased to 3.9% in February 2024, 3.8% in March 2024, and 3.9% in April 2024. By May 2024, it reached 4.0%, and continued climbing to 4.1% in June 2024. The rate peaked at 4.3% in July and August 2024, before moderating slightly to 4.1% in September 2024 and 4.1% in October 2024. It ended 2024 at 4.2% in November and 4.1% in December.

**Early 2025 Trends (January - March 2025):**
In early 2025, the unemployment rate showed some volatility. It stood at 4.0% in January 2025, increased to 4.1% in February 2025, and reached 4.2% in March 2025.

Over the 24-month period, the unemployment rate increased from 3.5% in March 2023 to 4.2% in March 2025, representing a 0.7 percentage point increase. The number of unemployed Americans grew from approximately 5.8 million to 7.1 million during this period.

## Key Relationship and Context

The evolution of these two indicators reflects the Federal Reserve's dual mandate challenge. The aggressive rate hikes in 2022 and early 2023 (totaling 525 basis points from near-zero to 5.25-5.50%) were designed to combat inflation that had reached multi-decade highs. As intended, these higher borrowing costs gradually cooled the labor market, as evidenced by the rising unemployment rate from its historic lows.

The lag between monetary policy actions and labor market effects is clearly visible: the Fed stopped hiking rates in July 2023, but unemployment continued to rise through 2024 and into 2025. This demonstrates the well-documented transmission lag of monetary policy, which typically takes 12-24 months to fully impact the real economy.

By late 2024, with inflation moderating significantly (PCE inflation declined from 7.2% in June 2022 to 2.1% by September 2024), the Fed began cutting rates to prevent further labor market deterioration. However, the unemployment rate continued to drift higher into early 2025, suggesting that the full effects of the previous tightening cycle were still working through the economy.

The 24-month period thus captures a complete monetary policy cycle: the final phase of aggressive tightening, an extended pause to assess economic conditions, and the beginning of a normalization phase as the Fed sought to achieve a "soft landing" - bringing inflation down without triggering a recession or excessive unemployment.

      "url": "https://archive.yardeni.com/morning-briefing-2021/",
      "content": "This time has been different so far, as Debbie, Eric, and I have observed on numerous occasions since early 2022:  
(1) *Normalizing vs tightening monetary policy.* The tightening of monetary policy during 2022 and 2023 raised the federal funds rate by 525bps (*Fig. 5*). That was certainly among one of the biggest increases in this rate during monetary policy tightening cycles in history. However, the federal funds rate was raised from zero. So we’ve characterized some of the increase in the federal funds rate as normalizing rather than tightening monetary policy.  
(2) *Fed’s liquidity facilities.* As noted above, there was a mini-banking crisis last year. But thanks to the Fed’s liquidity facility, there has been no credit crunch and no recession. The Fed played Whac-a-Mole during the Great Financial Crisis (GFC) and again during the Great Virus Crisis (GVC), learning to stabilize the credit system rapidly by creating emergency liquidity facilities.The difference last year was that the Fed didn’t also lower the federal funds rate as it did during the GFC and GVC.
In other words, the Fed might be making a mistake rushing to cut the federal funds rate until inflation is sustainably at 2.0% given that Washington will be inflation-prone next year. For now, the federal funds futures market is currently discounting two and four rate cuts of 25bps over the next six and 12 months (*Fig. 5* and *Fig. 6*).  
And what about the stock market? Our year-end target of 5400 for the S&P 500 was exceeded on June 12. The index closed at 5567.19 on Friday. That’s another new record high. So far, the current bull market has proceeded even as the Fed raised the federal funds rate (*Fig. 7*). The federal funds rate was 3.08% on October 12, 2022, when the S&P troughed. It has been at 5.3% since July 27, 2023 yet stock prices continued to advance. This time, if the Fed lowers the federal funds rate to successfully avert a recession, the bull market is likely to continue. In the past, a falling federal funds rate didn’t always end bear markets because it confirmed that the economy was in a recession.
On January 15, that spread was 159 basis points, implying six such rate cuts. That 80-basis-point spread implied that the FOMC anticipated making three rate cuts of 25 basis points each, not six.  
We view the spread between the federal funds rate and the 2-year US Treasury note yield as another measure of the market’s forecast for the change in the federal funds rate over the next 12 months (*Fig. 2*). The latter closed at 4.72% on Friday, implying two rate cuts through March 2024. We think the latest quarterly SEP, coming out this Wednesday, might very well suggest two, rather than the December SEP’s three, rate cuts over this period, occurring later rather than sooner this year.  
So the markets are now more in sync with the FOMC’s projections than they were in mid-January. Both anticipate two or three cuts, either this year or by March 2025.

From a low of 0.00-0.25 in March 2020, the fed funds rate reached 5.25-5.50 by the end of 2023. As inflation subsided in 2024, three rate cuts occurred and the fed funds rate dropped to 4.25-4.50. A softening labor market in 2025 prompted two rate cuts, one in September and another in late October, lowering the rate to 3.75-4.00.
The fed funds rate remained relatively constant at 5.25-5.50 between July 2023 and September 2024, but the 30-year fixed mortgage rate fluctuated and peaked at 7.76% in November 2023 before dropping to 6.09% in September 2024. Although three fed funds rate cuts occurred in late 2024 between September and December, mortgage rates generally moved in the opposite direction, increasing from 6.09% in September to approximately 7.00% by December. In 2025, the fed funds rate remained unchanged from January through August while mortgage rates fluctuated slightly and the spread remained relatively steady at 2.5 percentage points.
The dramatic rise in the fed funds rate resulting from 11 rate increases that began in 2022 and continued into 2023 led to the fed funds rate exceeding the 10-Year Treasury Bond Yield in 2023 and 2024. An “inverted yield curve” occurred, with the 10-Year Treasury Bond Yield exceeding the 3-Month Treasury Bill Yield. In effect, short-term interest rates were higher than long-term interest rates, which created the inverted yield curve. In 2025, the spread has hovered around zero, indicating that the 10-Year Treasury Bond Yield was approximately equal to the fed funds rate.

Nevertheless, structural trade imbalances driven by consumption patterns, energy imports, and service exports mean that monetary policy alone cannot fully correct the deficit.

- **The funds rate is not "the economy"**: The transmission from rate changes to real economic activity operates with long and variable lags, typically 12-24 months. But when inflation began falling in 2024, the Fed pivoted to monetary easing. It enacted 1 percentage point in rate cuts over September to December, which brought the federal-funds rate back down to a target range of 4.25%-4.50%. That’s where rates stand today. Source: Federal Reserve, Morningstar. Data as of June 24, 2025.
Even though Fed tightening created only a minor drag on economic growth over 2023-24, inflation ended up falling dramatically anyway. This was because of supply-side improvement, which is unrelated to monetary policy. We expect the Fed to resume cutting in the second half of 2025 and continue cutting intermittently through the end of 2027.",

      "url": "https://www.bizinsider.org/federal-reserve-holds-interest-rates-steady-what-that-means-for-mortgages-credit-cards-and-more/",
      "content": "**More from Personal Finance:**[Consumer outlook sinks as recession fears take hold](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/03/11/amid-recession-fears-consumers-are-pessimistic-about-their-finances.html)[Here’s the inflation breakdown for February 2025](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/03/12/heres-the-inflation-breakdown-for-february-2025-in-one-chart.html)[This step is ‘really important’ for home sellers in 2025](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/03/12/how-to-price-your-home-to-sell-in-2025.html)  
The federal funds rate sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending, but also[influences many of the borrowing and savings rates](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/30/how-interest-rates-have-changed-over-the-last-12-months.html)Americans see every day.  
When the Fed hiked rates in 2022 and 2023, most consumer[borrowing costs](https://www.cnbc.com/debt/)quickly followed suit. Even though the central bank began to [lower its benchmark rate](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/12/18/fed-rate-decision-december-2024-.html)at the end of last year, consumer rates are still elevated, with credit card annual percentage rates down only slightly from an all-time high.  
“The pressure on household budgets is unrelenting,” said Greg McBride, chief financial analyst at Bankrate.com.  
As the federal funds rate comes down, consumers may see their borrowing costs decrease as well, making it cheaper to borrow money to purchase a house or a car.
## Student loans  
[Federal student loan rates](https://www.cnbc.com/2016/11/10/how-you-could-save-under-trumps-student-loan-repayment-plan.html)are fixed, as well, so most borrowers are somewhat shielded from Fed moves and recent economic turmoil.  
Undergraduate students who took out direct federal student loans for the 2024-25 academic year are paying[6.53%](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/14/education-dept-announces-2024-25-interest-rates-on-student-loans.html), up from 5.50% in 2023-24. Interest rates for the upcoming school year will be based in part on the May auction of the[10-year Treasury note](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/US10Y/).  
Private student loans tend to have a variable rate tied to the prime, Treasury bill or another rate index.
## Savings  
On the upside, “savings rates really haven’t changed all that much, that’s the good news,” McBride said. “Savings rates are still at attractive levels and the top yields are still well in excess of inflation.”  
While the central bank has no direct influence on deposit rates, the yields tend to be correlated to changes in the target federal funds rate.  
Top-yielding online[savings](https://www.cnbc.com/savings/)accounts currently pay 4.4%, on average, according to Bankrate. Although that’s down from roughly 5% last year, it is well above the annualinflation rate of 2.8%.",

## What Fed Funds and CPI Capture  
The fed funds rate is the overnight interbank lending rate that the [FOMC](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm) targets to influence broader financial conditions. The [FOMC](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm) sets a target range (currently 3.50 to 3.75 percent in April 2026 after the December 2024 cut to that level). The actual effective rate (the volume-weighted average of overnight transactions) typically trades within 5 to 15 basis points of the midpoint of the target range. The rate transmits to bank lending rates, mortgage rates, corporate borrowing rates, and asset valuations through standard arbitrage relationships.  
Headline CPI measures the change in consumer prices over the past 12 months. The [Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov) releases the data monthly, typically two weeks after the reference month ends. The April 2026 release was on May 12 (showing March data); the upcoming June 11 release will show April data. CPI is the most-cited single inflation measure for headlines and policy purposes, although the Fed officially targets PCE inflation. The relationship between fed funds and CPI is the most fundamental policy diagnostic in monetary economics.

Over the last 24 months (approximately March 2023 to March 2025), both the federal funds rate and the US unemployment rate have shown significant evolution, reflecting the Federal Reserve's monetary policy response to inflation and the resulting labor market dynamics.

## Federal Funds Rate Evolution (March 2023 - March 2025)

**The Tightening Phase (March 2023 - July 2023):**
The Federal Reserve continued its aggressive rate hiking campaign in early 2023. In March 2023, the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to a target range of 4.75% - 5.00%. This was followed by another 25 basis point increase in May 2023, bringing the rate to 5.00% - 5.25%. The final rate hike of the cycle occurred in July 2023, with a 25 basis point increase to 5.25% - 5.50%, marking a 22-year high.

**The Extended Pause (July 2023 - September 2024):**
After reaching the peak rate of 5.25% - 5.50% in July 2023, the Federal Reserve held rates steady for over a year. The FOMC paused rates at eight consecutive meetings between July 2023 and July 2024, maintaining the 5.25% - 5.50% target range. During this period, the effective federal funds rate remained at approximately 5.33%.

**The Cutting Cycle Begins (September 2024 - March 2025):**
In September 2024, the Fed initiated its first rate cut in nearly three years with a significant 50 basis point reduction, bringing the rate to 4.75% - 5.00%. This was followed by two additional 25 basis point cuts: one in November 2024 (to 4.50% - 4.75%) and another in December 2024 (to 4.25% - 4.50%). The Fed then held rates steady at 4.25% - 4.50% through January and March 2025 meetings.

By March 2025, the federal funds rate stood at 4.25% - 4.50%, representing a cumulative reduction of 100 basis points from the peak, though still significantly elevated compared to pre-2022 levels.

## US Unemployment Rate Evolution (March 2023 - March 2025)

**Low and Stable Period (March 2023 - July 2023):**
The unemployment rate remained remarkably low during the first half of 2023. In March 2023, it stood at 3.5%, and reached a 50-year low of 3.4% in April 2023. The rate remained between 3.4% and 3.7% through July 2023, with June 2023 at 3.6% and July 2023 at 3.5%.

**Gradual Increase Phase (August 2023 - December 2023):**
Beginning in August 2023, the unemployment rate began a gradual upward trend. It increased to 3.8% in August, September, and October 2023, before settling at 3.7% for November and December 2023.

**Continued Rise (January 2024 - December 2024):**
Throughout 2024, the unemployment rate continued its upward trajectory. It remained at 3.7% in January 2024, then increased to 3.9% in February 2024, 3.8% in March 2024, and 3.9% in April 2024. By May 2024, it reached 4.0%, and continued climbing to 4.1% in June 2024. The rate peaked at 4.3% in July and August 2024, before moderating slightly to 4.1% in September 2024 and 4.1% in October 2024. It ended 2024 at 4.2% in November and 4.1% in December.

**Early 2025 Trends (January - March 2025):**
In early 2025, the unemployment rate showed some volatility. It stood at 4.0% in January 2025, increased to 4.1% in February 2025, and reached 4.2% in March 2025.

Over the 24-month period, the unemployment rate increased from 3.5% in March 2023 to 4.2% in March 2025, representing a 0.7 percentage point increase. The number of unemployed Americans grew from approximately 5.8 million to 7.1 million during this period.

## Key Relationship and Context

The evolution of these two indicators reflects the Federal Reserve's dual mandate challenge. The aggressive rate hikes in 2022 and early 2023 (totaling 525 basis points from near-zero to 5.25-5.50%) were designed to combat inflation that had reached multi-decade highs. As intended, these higher borrowing costs gradually cooled the labor market, as evidenced by the rising unemployment rate from its historic lows.

The lag between monetary policy actions and labor market effects is clearly visible: the Fed stopped hiking rates in July 2023, but unemployment continued to rise through 2024 and into 2025. This demonstrates the well-documented transmission lag of monetary policy, which typically takes 12-24 months to fully impact the real economy.

By late 2024, with inflation moderating significantly (PCE inflation declined from 7.2% in June 2022 to 2.1% by September 2024), the Fed began cutting rates to prevent further labor market deterioration. However, the unemployment rate continued to drift higher into early 2025, suggesting that the full effects of the previous tightening cycle were still working through the economy.

The 24-month period thus captures a complete monetary policy cycle: the final phase of aggressive tightening, an extended pause to assess economic conditions, and the beginning of a normalization phase as the Fed sought to achieve a "soft landing" - bringing inflation down without triggering a recession or excessive unemployment.

**July 2026:** The total stock of credit operations in Brazil's National Financial System (SFN) reached **R$7.4 trillion** (approximately R$7,372 trillion), representing a 0.3% increase from June 2026 and a 9.5% increase over 12 months. This breaks down as:
- Credit to legal entities (corporations): R$2.7 trillion (decreased 0.7% in the month)
- Credit to individuals (households): R$4.6 trillion (increased 0.8% in the month)

**June 2026:** Total credit operations reached **R$7.355.80 billion** (R$7.4 trillion), with:
- Business credit: R$2.749 trillion
- Household credit: R$4.606.8 trillion

**May 2026:** The outstanding balance of credit operations reached **R$7.3 trillion**, growing 0.6% from the previous month.

## Earlier Periods:

**December 2025:** Total credit in Brazil reached **R$7.1 trillion** ($1.37 trillion USD), with bank lending increasing 10.2% in 2025 overall. This exceeded the Central Bank's forecast of 9.4% expansion.
- Household lending: increased 11.6% in 2025
- Corporate credit: grew 8.1% in 2025

**November 2024:** Total SFN credit operations reached **R$6.3 trillion**, growing 10.7% year-on-year.

## Credit Composition:

The Brazilian credit system includes:
- **Free credit** (market-based): R$4.2 trillion (approximately 57% of total)
- **Directed credit** (subsidized/earmarked): R$3.2 trillion (approximately 43% of total), which includes housing finance via Caixa Econômica Federal, rural lending via Banco do Brasil and BNDES, and social infrastructure financing

## Additional Context:

The aggregate credit-to-GDP ratio stood at approximately **162.3% of GDP** as of March 2026, with total credit extended to the non-financial sector reaching R$21.0 trillion when including all forms of credit beyond traditional banking operations.

The Brazilian financial system also includes Brazil's National Cooperative Credit System (SNCC), which crossed R$1 trillion in assets in 2025, with a credit portfolio of R$455 billion.

      "url": "https://captaincompliance.com/education/brazils-superior-court-draws-a-hard-line-on-credit-bureau-data-sharing-what-privacy-professionals-must-understand/",
      "content": "## Not All Credit Data Is Legally Equal  
One of the ruling’s most practically useful contributions is its insistence that the Brazilian credit market acknowledge what privacy professionals have long understood: “credit data” is not a single homogeneous category, and its legal treatment must reflect the meaningful differences between its constituent types.  
The court implicitly distinguished between three layers of data that commonly circulate in credit-related contexts:  
**Credit scores and statistical risk models.** A score derived from aggregated variables expresses a probability, not a personal identity. Brazilian case law has long accepted that scoring models may be operated without individual consent, provided that transparency, proportionality, and non-discrimination principles are respected. The LGPD’s credit protection basis is well-suited to this use.  
**Credit history and payment behaviour.** Information about past and present payment conduct is regulated in Brazil primarily through the Cadastro Positivo — the Positive Credit Registry — which establishes a specific framework for the inclusion and use of payment history data, along with defined rights for data subjects. This layer operates under its own regulatory architecture.
## Presumed Moral Damages: The Litigation Dimension  
Beyond its regulatory significance, the STJ’s decision carries a civil liability dimension that fundamentally changes the risk calculus for credit bureaus and the organisations that receive data from them.  
The court confirmed that the unlawful sharing of identifiable registration data constitutes a basis for presumed moral damages — that is, damages that the affected individual does not need to prove through evidence of financial loss, denial of credit, or other concrete harm. The violation of the individual’s informational self-determination — their right to control how personal data about them circulates — is itself the harm.  
The implications of this holding are considerable. Brazil’s credit ecosystem involves millions of data subjects and industrial-scale data sharing. An organisation that has been operating on the assumption that the credit protection legal basis covers all downstream sharing is not facing a single regulatory investigation — it is potentially facing systematic litigation exposure across its entire customer base, without any requirement that individual claimants demonstrate concrete injury.
## Audit All Data Flows in Brazil and Out of Brazil  
The STJ’s decision in REsp 2.201.694/SP does not come with a transitional grace period. Its effects on the legality of existing data sharing arrangements are immediate, and organisations that have not yet assessed their exposure face compounding risk with each passing month. The following are the priority actions for privacy professionals operating in or advising the Brazilian credit market:  
**Audit all data flows involving identifiable registration data.** Map every instance in which your organisation shares — or receives — identifiable consumer registration data with third parties. Identify the legal basis relied upon for each transfer and assess whether that basis survives the court’s reasoning. Flows that were previously justified solely by reference to credit protection will, in many cases, require a different legal footing or must be suspended pending consent collection.  
**Reassess data sharing agreements.** Contracts with third-party recipients of identifiable data should be reviewed in light of the ruling. Representations about lawful processing basis, downstream use restrictions, and liability allocation may all require revision. New agreements should be structured with the STJ’s framework explicitly in mind.",
